analysis.one_liner: Doubles and makes permanent the corporate research tax credit and adds a credit for worker science training.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to double the corporate research tax credit drew 61 cosponsors but never received a Senate Finance Committee vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have doubled the federal tax credit for corporate research and development from 20% to 40% of qualifying spending, made that credit permanent (it has historically been extended only a few years at a time), and expanded it to joint research consortia. It would also have created a new credit, capped at $500 million a year, paying employers for continuing education of their science and engineering workers, and directed the Treasury Department to study further tax breaks for innovation investment. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations that spend heavily on research and development — pharmaceutical, technology, aerospace, and defense companies among them — would have received a doubled, permanent tax credit on qualifying research spending. Employers of scientists and engineers would have gained a new credit covering workers' continuing education. The stated public rationale is that stronger innovation incentives keep high-value research and the jobs around it in the United States.

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the research credit rate from 20% to 40% of qualifying research spending and removes its expiration date, giving companies a larger and more predictable subsidy for R&D.
Expands the credit to cover expenses of general research consortia, not just energy research consortia, letting joint industry research efforts qualify.
Creates a new business credit, capped at $500 million per year nationally, for employers to cover continuing education in science or engineering for their employees.

Directs Treasury to study making the credit more generous and to compare U.S. tax treatment of long-term innovation investment, capital gains, and corporate rates with other nations — groundwork for further tax breaks.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through the revenue the government would forgo. Doubling the rate and making the research credit permanent would convert a temporary, annually renewed tax break into a large, ongoing corporate tax expenditure with no offsetting revenue in the bill.

drawbacks.text: Doubling the credit rate and making it permanent would sharply increase the cost to the Treasury, reducing federal revenue available for other purposes, and the bill includes no way to pay for it.
The credit is claimed by companies and subsidizes research spending they would likely undertake in part anyway; the benefit reaches workers and the public only indirectly through company decisions.

The new continuing-education credit flows to employers rather than directly to workers, so its benefit to employees depends on employers expanding training rather than simply claiming the credit for training they already provide.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is designed around large, permanent tax subsidies to research-performing corporations, with any public benefit — more innovation, more high-skill jobs — indirect and unquantified in the bill itself. The main provision doubles an existing corporate credit with no revenue offset, while the one provision aimed at workers is small (capped at $500 million a year) and routed through employers. On balance the measure is a corporate tax package with a modest worker-training add-on.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2006 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never brought it up, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Pete Domenici introduced the bill on January 26, 2006, with 45 original cosponsors from both parties.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The bill ultimately attracted 61 cosponsors — 33 Democrats and 28 Republicans — giving it the backing of a clear majority of the Senate.

The Finance Committee took no further action; the only subsequent record entry is a repeat of the sponsor's introductory remarks in September 2006, and the bill never received a markup or a vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, taxpayers kept the revenue that a doubled, permanent research credit would have cost, and research-performing corporations did not receive the larger subsidy — though they retained the existing version of the credit under prior law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, in the form of unspent revenue

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start: its 61 cosponsors split 33 Democrats to 28 Republicans, and opposition never registered as votes — the bill simply stalled in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have doubled the research tax credit rate to 40% and made it permanent, a large and predictable subsidy to companies that already spend the most on R&D. Its cost would be borne by general taxpayers through forgone federal revenue.

A new credit would reimburse employers up to a $500 million national cap for workers' science and engineering continuing education. Workers benefit only if employers expand training rather than claim the credit for existing programs.

industries.industry: Continuing education and professional training providers
industries.note: A federally subsidized stream of employer-funded course enrollment would create new demand for technical training programs.
